title: What if you sank to the bottom of the deepest lake?

hook.banner: What's at the bottom of Lake Baikal?

narration.heading: Lake Baikal
narration.text: You're sinking into the deepest lake on Earth. And it's full of life found nowhere else.

narration.heading: A fifth of it all
narration.text: Lake Baikal, in Siberia, holds more than a fifth of all the fresh water on Earth's surface.

narration.heading: Crystal clear
narration.text: In winter, you can see thirty to forty metres down through its crystal-clear water.

narration.heading: Found nowhere else
narration.text: Look closer. More than three hundred and fifty kinds of tiny amphipods live here, and nowhere else.

narration.heading: See-through fish
narration.text: Below a hundred metres, see-through golomyanka fish drift by. Baikal's seals live mostly on them.

narration.heading: 300 m down
narration.text: Past three hundred metres, the water stays at a steady three degrees, all year round.

narration.heading: The bottom
narration.text: One thousand six hundred and forty-two metres: the bottom. That's almost two Burj Khalifas deep.

narration.heading: The twist
narration.text: The twist? Baikal has oxygen all the way down, so fish live even here. The deepest freshwater fish anywhere.

narration.heading: The oldest lake
narration.text: And this lake is twenty-five to thirty million years old, the oldest on Earth. Which lake should we sink into next?

skit.text: Twenty-five million years old? And I thought my code was ancient.

titles: What if you sank to the bottom of the deepest lake?
Sinking 1,642 m to the bottom of Lake Baikal
youtube.description: Sink through Lake Baikal, the world's deepest and oldest lake, past amphipods and see-through golomyanka fish found nowhere else, to the bottom 1,642 metres down.

sources.claim: Lake Baikal is 1,642 m deep, the deepest and oldest lake (25–30 million years), holding 22–23% of the world's fresh surface water
Winter transparency reaches 30–40 m; below about 300 m the water is stable at 3.1–3.4 °C; the water is rich in oxygen even in deep sections
More than 350 endemic amphipod species and subspecies live in Baikal; golomyanka and certain sculpins are the deepest-living freshwater fish
Golomyankas have translucent bodies, live mostly below 100 m, and make up more than 90% of the Baikal seal's diet
The Baikal seal is endemic to Lake Baikal and feeds mainly on golomyanka
The Burj Khalifa's roof height is 828 m
